**Chemistry**

**Chapter 5: Chemical Bond**

**5.1 Formation of Magnesium Oxide**

In the NaH molecule, Na atom donates an electron to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and becomes Na+ with 8 electrons.

The H atom accepts that electron to get the electronic configuration of an inert gas and become H- with 2 electrons.

**Fig 5.06: Formation of Magnesium Oxide**

[DIAGRAM]
Caption: Fig 5.06: Formation of Magnesium Oxide
Callouts: Magnesium atom, Oxygen atom, Magnesium Oxide
Description: The diagram shows the formation of magnesium oxide from magnesium and oxygen atoms.

**5.2 Ionic Bonding**

Now, Na+ and H- come closer to form an ionic bond.

In the CaO molecule, Ca atom donates two electrons to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and becomes Ca2+ with 8 electrons.

The O atom accepts those electrons to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and become O- with 8 electrons.

**Ca → Ca2+ + 2e-**

The O atom accepts those electrons to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and become O- with 8 electrons.

**O + 2e- → O2-**

Now, Ca2+ and O2- come closer to form an ionic bond.

Notably, the metals belonging to Group 1 and 2 and the non-metals of Group 16 and 17 of the periodic table usually commit themselves to ionic bonding. Each rule has some exceptions. Here in this case, Al of Group-13 commits itself to ionic bonding. Other elements do not show this tendency to donate or accept electrons as they have too many electrons at their outermost energy level. As ionic bonding takes place through electrostatic force, it is very strong.

**5.3 Conclusion**

In conclusion, the formation of magnesium oxide is an example of ionic bonding, where the magnesium atom donates an electron to become a positively charged ion (Mg2+) and the oxygen atom accepts that electron to become a negatively charged ion (O2-). The resulting compound, magnesium oxide, is formed when the positively charged magnesium ion and the negatively charged oxygen ion come together to form an ionic bond.
